report:
## Conclusion

The answer is **yes**, not no. The evidence consistently shows that offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) increases HIV testing uptake compared to standard testing services.

### Key Evidence

1. **Systematic review and meta-analysis (2021)**: HIVST increased testing uptake overall (RR 2.09; 95% CI 1.69–2.58; p < 0.0001; 13 RCTs; moderate certainty evidence), with increases across facility-based, secondary distribution, and community-based models. ([The Lancet eClinicalMedicine](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext))

2. **Narrative review (2020)**: Numerous randomized controlled trials found that offering HIVST increases HIV testing rates. ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11904-020-00504-3))

3. **2024 review**: Self-testing increases the uptake of HIV testing overall and the frequency of testing among both key populations and the general population compared to standard testing services. ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352301824001875))

4. **RCT in Australia (FORTH)**: Access to free HIV self-tests doubled the frequency of HIV testing in high-risk gay and bisexual men compared to standard care. ([The Lancet Western Pacific](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanwpc/article/PIIS2666-6065(21)00123-1/fulltext))

### Summary

Across multiple systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and RCTs, the additional offer of HIV self-testing consistently leads to more people taking an HIV test, with effect sizes roughly doubling uptake. The evidence is robust and spans general populations, men who have sex with men, and other key populations.
